summary: Extends Dual-Stack Lite by moving network address and port translation from a central tunnel concentrator out to the client. This makes provider-side state simpler. It builds on RFC 6333.

plainLanguage.summary:
Lightweight 4over6 lets an IPv4-only customer use an IPv6-only network. It keeps the same tunnel as Dual-Stack Lite but moves the job of rewriting addresses and ports out of the provider's tunnel server and into the customer's own router.

The provider then keeps one record per customer instead of one record per connection, which cuts both the memory it needs and the connection logs it must keep. The customer side has to be provisioned with a public IPv4 address and a range of ports it is allowed to use.

questions: what does the lwaftr binding table contain
subtitle: Moving IPv4 address and port translation from the provider's tunnel server into the customer's router.

tldr.problem: In Dual-Stack Lite the provider's tunnel endpoint does network address translation, so it must keep a record for every live flow. For a provider with many customers that state is expensive to hold and expensive to log.
tldr.mechanism: Lightweight 4over6 moves the translation into the customer-side router, gives each customer a public IPv4 address together with a restricted range of ports, and leaves the tunnel endpoint holding one binding record per subscriber instead of one per flow.
tldr.outcome: The provider keeps per-subscriber state rather than per-flow state and needs no central NAT function. The cost is that every customer must be provisioned with an address and port set that the tunnel endpoint also knows about.

facts.label: Binding table entry
facts.value: IPv6 address, public IPv4 address and restricted port set

today: RFC 7596 is a Proposed Standard from July 2015 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends RFC 6333 rather than replacing it, and the document itself describes the work as architectural, leaving redundancy and provisioning policy out of scope.

sections.title: Why the DS-Lite Tunnel Endpoint Becomes Expensive
sections.content:
Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite), defined in RFC 6333, gives IPv4 access over an IPv6-only network. It uses two pieces. The B4 is a function on a dual-stack node, either a directly connected device or customer equipment, that builds an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel. The AFTR is the tunnel endpoint at the provider, combined with an IPv4-to-IPv4 network address translator.

Because the AFTR performs the translation, it hands out public IPv4 addresses and ports as traffic arrives and has to keep a record for every live flow, in the form of active NAT sessions. For a service provider with a large number of B4 clients, the size and cost of scaling the AFTR can quickly become prohibitive. Per-flow state also puts a large logging overhead on providers in countries where logging is a legal requirement.

Lightweight 4over6, abbreviated lw4o6, keeps the same tunnel but relocates the NAPT44 function from the centralized AFTR to the distributed B4s. The RFC lists the benefits: NAPT44 is already widely supported in customer equipment, so the provider does not need a centralized NAT44 function; the state held centrally drops from per-flow to per-subscriber, which reduces the memory and processing power the AFTR needs; and the reduced state also greatly reduces logging overhead. Because the translation no longer sits in the middle, the provider's IPv6 and IPv4 addressing plans stay independent of each other, so flexible IPv4 and IPv6 addressing schemes can be deployed.

The tunneling mechanism itself does not change. What the document adds is the configuration and provisioning needed to make the change, in the spirit of the address-plus-port approach that RFC 7040 defines, extended here to allow address sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: DS-Lite gives IPv4 service over an IPv6 network by rewriting addresses at the provider's tunnel server. That server has to remember every live connection, so it gets expensive to run and expensive to log. Lightweight 4over6 does the rewriting in the customer's own router instead, and the provider remembers only one record per customer.

sections.title: The Lightweight 4over6 Architecture
sections.content:
The lw4o6 architecture has three main components. The lwB4 performs the NAPT44 function and the IPv4-to-IPv6 encapsulation and decapsulation. The lwAFTR performs only the encapsulation and decapsulation; it does not translate addresses. The third component is the provisioning system, which tells the lwB4 which IPv4 address and port set to use. The RFC allows the lwB4 to be a directly connected device, customer premises equipment, or a function inside a host.

The lwAFTR needs to know the binding between the IPv6 address of each subscriber and the IPv4 address and port set allocated to that subscriber. It uses this information to filter traffic upstream and to encapsulate traffic downstream. The RFC stresses that this is per-subscriber state, in contrast to the per-flow state kept by a regular AFTR.

There is a consequence: the information held by the provisioning mechanism and the information held by the lwAFTR must be synchronized. The precise mechanism for doing that is out of scope for the document, but the requirement stands.

The solution allows the assignment of either a full or a shared IPv4 address to requesting customer equipment, and it extends the mechanism of RFC 7040, which provides for a full IPv4 address only. The RFC places the approach in the family of binding approaches and describes it as a variant of the address-plus-port scheme, in what RFC 6346 calls Binding Table Mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Three pieces make up the system. The customer's router translates addresses and wraps IPv4 packets inside IPv6. The provider's tunnel server only wraps and unwraps them. A provisioning system tells the customer's router which public address and port range it may use, and the provider's server keeps the matching record.

sections.title: Provisioning the lwB4 with DHCPv6
sections.content:
With DS-Lite the B4 needs a single DS-Lite-specific parameter, the IPv6 address of the AFTR, and can take its IPv4 address from the well-known range 192.0.0.0/29. lw4o6 needs four parameters: the IPv6 address of the lwAFTR, the IPv4 external address for NAPT44, the restricted port set to use for NAPT44, and the IPv6 binding prefix.

The lwB4 must implement DHCPv6-based configuration using OPTION_S46_CONT_LW, as described in Section 5.3 of RFC 7598. The lifetime of the softwire and of the derived configuration, such as the shared or full IPv4 address, is therefore tied to the lifetime of the DHCPv6 lease. If stateful IPv4 configuration or further IPv4 information is needed, DHCP 4o6 from RFC 7341 must be used.

The binding prefix lets the customer edge identify which prefix to use as the source of the tunnel. On receipt of its parameters the lwB4 performs a longest-prefix match between the binding prefix and its currently active IPv6 prefixes; the result forms the subnet used to source the tunnel, and the full /128 address is then constructed in the same manner as in RFC 7597.

The construction has four parts: an operator assigned prefix, which is the IPv6 prefix allocated to the client and is right-padded with zeros to 64 bits if the prefix is shorter; zero padding; the public IPv4 address allocated to the client; and the Port Set ID, which is allocated to the client and left-padded with zeros to 16 bits, and is all zeros if no PSID is provisioned.

An lwB4 must support dynamic port-restricted IPv4 address provisioning, and the number of a-bits should be zero, so that each lwB4 is given a single contiguous port set. Unless the lwB4 is being given a full IPv4 address of its own, the RFC recommends that PSIDs containing the system ports 0-1023 are not allocated, because those reserved ports are more likely to be held by middleware.

If the lwB4's IPv6 encapsulation source address changes, for example because the DHCPv6 lease expired, the dynamic provisioning process must be started again. If the public IPv4 address or the PSID changes for any reason, the lwB4 must flush its NAT table.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer router has to learn four things: where the provider's tunnel server is, which public IPv4 address it may use, which ports it may use from, and which of its own IPv6 prefixes to build the tunnel from. Those settings arrive over DHCPv6, so they expire together with the lease. The tunnel source address is then built from the operator's prefix, the public IPv4 address and a port set identifier.

sections.title: The lwB4 Data Plane
sections.content:
Hosts behind the lwB4 send IPv4 packets carrying addresses from the private range of RFC 1918. When the lwB4 receives such a packet, it performs the NAPT44 function on the source address and port, using the public IPv4 address and a port number from the allocated port set. It then encapsulates the packet with an IPv6 header: the destination IPv6 address is the lwAFTR's address and the source is the lwB4's own IPv6 tunnel endpoint address. The encapsulated packet is forwarded to the configured lwAFTR.

On the way back, the lwB4 decapsulates the IPv4 packet from the IPv6 packet and translates the destination address and port using its local NAT table. If the IPv6 source address does not match the configured lwAFTR address, the packet must be discarded. If the decapsulated IPv4 packet does not match the lwB4's configuration, because of an invalid destination IPv4 address or port, the packet must be dropped; an ICMPv4 error of type 3, code 13, Destination Unreachable with Communication Administratively Prohibited, may be sent back to the lwAFTR, and the ICMP policy should be configurable.

The lwB4 also carries the duties of an ordinary home router. It performs application layer gateway functions for protocols such as SIP and FTP, and handles NAT traversal for internal hosts through mechanisms such as UPnP with an Internet Gateway Device, the NAT Port Mapping Protocol, manual binding configuration and PCP. The RFC calls this typical for NAPT44 gateways available today.

Address sharing creates one problem in this data path. If IPv4 hosts behind different lwB4s that share an address send fragments to the same destination outside the lw4o6 domain, the destination may see the same IPv4 fragmentation identifier from both and reassemble the fragments incorrectly. The identifier is a 16-bit field and could be rewritten to fall within the allocated port set, but splitting the identifier space that way would raise the chance of a reassembly collision for every connection through the lwB4.
sections.plainLanguage: Outgoing packets have their address and port rewritten and are wrapped inside an IPv6 packet for the trip to the provider. Incoming packets are unwrapped and translated back. Anything from an unexpected source is dropped. The customer router also does the job an ordinary home router does, including helping applications through the address translation.

sections.title: The lwAFTR Binding Table and Data Plane
sections.content:
The lwAFTR maintains an address binding table. Unlike the DS-Lite extended binding table, which is a 5-tuple NAT table, each entry in the lw4o6 binding table holds three values: the IPv6 address of a single lwB4, the public IPv4 address, and the restricted port set. The entry has two jobs: choosing the IPv6 encapsulation for inbound IPv4 packets destined to that lwB4, and validating outbound IPv4-in-IPv6 packets received from it. Because the lwAFTR does not perform NAT, it needs no session entries.

When a packet arrives from an lwB4, the lwAFTR decapsulates the IPv6 header and verifies the source addresses and port against the binding table. If the source IPv4 and IPv6 addresses both match a single entry, and the source port is inside the allowed port set for that entry, the packet is forwarded to the IPv4 destination. If no match is found, for example because there is no matching IPv4 address entry or the port is out of range, the lwAFTR must discard the packet or apply a policy such as redirection; an ICMPv6 error of type 1, code 5 may be sent back to the requesting lwB4, and the ICMP policy should be configurable.

For an inbound IPv4 packet the lwAFTR uses the IPv4 destination address and port to find the destination lwB4's IPv6 address in the binding table. On a match it encapsulates the packet, with the lwAFTR's IPv6 address as source and the matched IPv6 address as destination, and forwards the packet natively over the IPv6 network. With no match, the lwAFTR must discard the packet, and an ICMPv4 error of type 3, code 1, Destination Unreachable Host Unreachable, may be sent back.

The lwAFTR must support hairpinning, so that two lwB4s served by the same lwAFTR can reach each other: the packet from one is decapsulated and re-encapsulated for the other. The hairpinning policy must be configurable.

The binding table has to be created as part of the port-restricted address provisioning process, or, if the lwAFTR takes no part in that process, synchronized by other means such as an out-of-band static update. For all provisioning processes, the lifetime of binding table entries must be synchronized with the lifetime of the address allocations.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider's tunnel server keeps one row per customer, holding the customer's IPv6 address, its public IPv4 address and its port range. It checks outgoing packets against that row and uses it to wrap incoming packets for the customer. It never rewrites addresses itself, and it can pass traffic between two customers behind the same server.

sections.title: ICMP Processing in a Shared Address
sections.content:
Both the lwAFTR and the lwB4 must handle ICMPv6 as described in RFC 2473. ICMPv4 does not work in an address-sharing environment without special handling, and because lw4o6 shares addresses using port sets, it needs specific ICMP handling that DS-Lite does not.

The lwAFTR handles inbound ICMP messages in a defined order. It checks the ICMP type field first. For echo reply and echo request, types 0 and 8, it takes the value of the ICMP Identifier field as the source port and uses that value to look up the binding table for an encapsulation destination; if a match is found the ICMP packet is forwarded to the IPv6 address stored in the entry, and otherwise it must be discarded. For any other type, it uses the method described in REQ-3 of RFC 5508 to locate the source port within the transport-layer header in the ICMP packet's data field; the destination IPv4 address and the extracted source port are then used for the binding table lookup, and a match means the packet is forwarded to the IPv6 address in the entry, while no match means it must be discarded. All other inbound ICMPv4 messages must be discarded. The ICMP policy should be configurable.

The lwB4 must implement the ICMP forwarding requirements of RFC 5508. For ICMP echo request packets originating from the private IPv4 network, it should use the method described in RFC 6346 and use an available port from its port set as the ICMP identifier.

There is one more rule for the lwB4. If it receives an ICMPv6 error message of type 1, code 5 from the lwAFTR, it reads this as meaning that no matching entry was found in the lwAFTR's binding table, so the IPv4 payload is not being forwarded. It may then start the dynamic port-restricted provisioning process again, and that policy should be configurable. Because such a message could be forged, the lwB4 must check that the source address is the configured lwAFTR address and discard the message if it is not. An operator can also apply network ingress filtering as described in RFC 2827.
sections.plainLanguage: Error messages are hard to route when several customers share one address. The provider's server works out which customer a message belongs to by reading the port number, taken from the ICMP identifier field for echo messages and from the transport header carried inside the message for everything else. Messages that match nobody are dropped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As the port space for a subscriber shrinks because of address sharing, the randomness in the port numbers that subscriber uses falls sharply. It becomes much easier for an attacker to guess the port number in use, which can lead to attacks ranging from reduced throughput to broken connections or data corruption.

A contiguous port set does not reduce this threat. Non-contiguous port sets do, because they can be generated in a pseudorandom way, and the improved randomness only helps when the attacker is outside the lw4o6 domain and therefore does not know the port-set generation algorithm.

The lwAFTR must rate-limit ICMPv6 error messages, to defend against denial-of-service attacks generated by an abusive user.

Security considerations for the provisioning protocol in use apply unchanged to lw4o6, and lw4o6 adds no further security considerations of its own for those protocols. The RFC also points to Section 13 of RFC 6269, which discusses the issues with IP address sharing and applies to this solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Fewer ports per customer means port numbers are easier to guess, and a guessed port can be used to break or corrupt a connection. Spreading the ports out at random helps, as long as the attacker does not know how the port set was made. The provider must also limit how many ICMP error messages it sends.
